title: Cervical Spondylosis (Neck Pain): Ayurvedic View, Causes, Posture, Exercises & Care
excerpt: Neck stiffness, pain spreading to the shoulders, tingling in the hands or dizziness — in this age of hours on phones and computers, cervical pain has become very common. Learn what cervical spondylosis is, how Ayurveda understands it as “Manyastambha/Grivagraha”, correct posture, exercises, diet, safe home measures and when you must see a doctor right away.
content:
Pain on turning the neck as soon as you wake up, heaviness in the shoulders all day, and sometimes tingling down to the fingers — such complaints are now common even among young people of 25–30. Looking down at the phone for long periods, sitting at a computer for hours, a high pillow and little physical activity are big causes; with age, the bones and cushions of the neck also wear.

The good news is that in most people, correct posture, regular exercise, a better routine and proper treatment control the pain to a large extent. This article is for information only — take any treatment only on the advice of your vaidya or doctor.

What is cervical spondylosis?

The neck part of the spine has seven bones (cervical vertebrae), with cushions (discs) between them. Over time, or from poor posture and excess strain, these discs lose water and become thinner, and bony outgrowths (osteophytes) can form on the edges of the bones — this wear is called cervical spondylosis. Its main forms are:

  • Neck pain and stiffness only — the most common; pain on turning the neck, heaviness up to the shoulders and back of the head
  • Pressure on a nerve (radiculopathy) — pain, tingling or numbness travelling from the shoulder down the arm to the fingers
  • Pressure on the spinal cord (myelopathy) — less common but serious; weakness in the hands, difficulty buttoning or writing, unsteady walking

Remember: “spondylosis” on an X-ray is very common with age and is not always the cause of pain. Treatment is decided more by your symptoms and examination than by the report.

The Ayurvedic view

In Ayurveda, stiffness and pain of the neck is called Manyastambha (stiffening of the neck muscles and channels) or Grivagraha, and it is counted among the Vatavyadhi (diseases of Vata dosha). Madhava Nidana describes its cause very precisely:

दिवास्वप्नासनस्थानविकृतोर्ध्वनिरीक्षणैः ।
मन्यास्तम्भं प्रकुरुते स एव श्लेष्मणावृतः ॥
— Madhava Nidana, Vatavyadhi Nidana (Chapter 22)

Meaning: Sleeping during the day, sitting or standing in a faulty way, and keeping the neck raised unnaturally while looking up — through these the same Vata, covered by Kapha, produces Manyastambha (stiffness of the neck).

So thousands of years ago Ayurveda already saw “wrong posture” as a major cause — today, looking down at phones and sitting badly at computers do the same. Mainly Vata (pain, tingling, dryness, wear) and often Kapha (heaviness, stiffness, morning stiffness) are involved. So the aim of treatment is — to calm Vata, remove the obstruction of Kapha, nourish the tissues and correct wrong habits.

Main causes and risk factors

  • Looking down at a phone or sitting badly at a laptop/computer for long periods
  • Natural wear of the discs and joints with age
  • A very high or very hard pillow, sleeping on the stomach
  • Carrying heavy loads on the head, jerky work, or an old neck injury
  • Little physical activity, weak neck and shoulder muscles, smoking
  • Stress, too little sleep, cold wind or a direct blast of AC (Vata-aggravating factors)

Symptoms and tests

  • Neck pain and stiffness, especially in the morning or after staying in one position for long
  • Pain spreading to the shoulders, between the shoulder blades or to the back of the head
  • Headache starting from the back of the neck
  • Clicking sounds on turning the neck or reduced movement
  • Tingling, numbness or weakness in the arm or fingers
  • In some people, mild dizziness or imbalance on turning the neck

The doctor first checks your neck movement, strength, reflexes and sensation in the hands. If needed, a neck X-ray may be advised, and if there are signs of nerve pressure or weakness, an MRI; sometimes a nerve conduction study (NCV) too. If there is dizziness, the ears, BP and other causes are also checked.

Diet: what to eat, what to avoid

In cervical pain the aim of diet is — to calm Vata, keep digestion healthy and nourish the bones and muscles. According to Ayurveda, warm, fresh, lightly unctuous (with a little ghee or oil) and easily digestible food is considered beneficial in Vata disorders.

What to eat

  • Fresh, warm, cooked food — dalia, khichdi, moong dal, wheat, rice
  • Cooked vegetables such as bottle gourd, ridge gourd, pumpkin, carrot, spinach; ginger, garlic, cumin and turmeric in food
  • A little desi ghee or sesame oil in food (ask your doctor if you have heart disease or high cholesterol)
  • Milk, curd, paneer, sesame, ragi — for calcium (whatever suits you)
  • Soaked almonds, walnuts, seasonal fruits such as papaya, pomegranate, apple
  • Lukewarm water through the day; some time in the sun — for vitamin D

What to avoid

  • Very cold, stale food straight from the fridge and cold drinks
  • Dry, very rough and packaged food, too much tea or coffee
  • Maida, fried food, junk food, excess sugar
  • Smoking and alcohol — these can increase disc wear and pain

Correct posture and daily routine

  • Raise your phone to eye level; do not look down at it with a bent neck for long
  • Computer screen in front of your eyes, back straight and supported on the chair; get up every 30–40 minutes and move your neck and shoulders
  • A thin, soft pillow that supports the curve of the neck; do not sleep on your stomach
  • Do not carry a heavy bag on one shoulder; do not carry heavy loads on the head
  • While driving, keep the seat and headrest adjusted; take breaks on long journeys
  • Avoid daytime sleep, sleep on time; protect your neck from cold wind and direct AC

Yoga, pranayama and neck exercises

Slowly bending the neck forward-back and side to side (without jerks), rolling the shoulders, the chin-tuck exercise, Bhujangasana, Makarasana, Marjari asana, Tadasana and Anulom-Vilom and Bhramari pranayama are considered helpful. Caution: do not rotate the neck fast in circles; avoid postures that load the neck such as Halasana, Sarvangasana and Shirshasana; if there is weakness in the hands, severe pain or dizziness, stop exercising and see a doctor; learn yoga only from a trained teacher.

Safe home measures

  • Warm fomentation: gentle warmth for 10–15 minutes with a hot-water bag or warm towel — take care not to burn the skin
  • Gentle oil massage: a very light-handed massage of the neck and shoulders with lukewarm sesame oil, followed by a warm bath
  • Posture reminder: set an alarm every half hour on the phone/computer to get up and move your neck and shoulders
  • Stress and sleep: Bhramari or deep breathing before bed, so that shoulder tension eases

Jerking the neck to make it “crack”, getting the neck “set” by an untrained person or vigorous massage can be dangerous — avoid them. Do not take painkillers on your own for long periods.

Ayurvedic treatment — with caution

Ayurveda mentions many medicines for Vatavyadhi and Manyastambha, such as — Rasna, Shallaki, Ashwagandha, Bala, Dashamoola, Guduchi and classical formulations such as Yogaraja Guggulu. After examination, when suitable, Nasya karma, and at the clinic Agnikarma, Marma therapy, cupping therapy, Viddhakarma, acupressure and yoga and pranayama may be advised. But:

  • Which medicine or therapy, in what dose and for how long — the vaidya decides only after looking at the stage of the disease, age, prakriti, pulse, test reports and current medicines.
  • Do not stop your current medicines on your own; make any change only on your doctor’s advice.
  • Some medicines such as guggulu do not suit everyone and can change the effect of other drugs, so tell your vaidya the list of all your medicines; avoid “miracle painkillers” without a name or address — they often contain hidden steroids.
  • In pregnancy, breastfeeding, children and the elderly, any medicine or therapy only on the advice of a vaidya/doctor. Be wary of claims like “cervical cured from the root”.

When to see a doctor immediately

  • Increasing weakness in the hands, dropping things, difficulty buttoning or writing
  • Unsteady walking or weakness/numbness in the legs
  • A change in control of urine or stool — go to hospital immediately
  • Neck pain after an accident, fall or injury
  • A stiff neck with high fever, or pain with unexplained weight loss
  • Neck-shoulder pain that spreads to the chest, left arm or jaw with sweating or breathlessness — this may be a heart problem

Summary — points to remember

  • Cervical pain is common and in most people is controlled with proper care
  • Most important is correct posture — phone at eye level, regular breaks, a thin pillow
  • Gentle daily neck and shoulder exercises without jerks; no postures that load the neck
  • Warm, fresh, easily digestible food; less cold, stale and dry food
  • Do not delay if there is weakness in the arms or legs or a change in urine/stool; medicines and therapies only under a qualified vaidya’s supervision
